scene_description: Topic ideation for course papers, theses, research proposals, journal submissions and grant applications. Produces specific research questions that are falsifiable, add academic value, and are feasible to run.

questions.question: What is your discipline or course area? (You can go as specific as the subfield, e.g. communication studies, modern Chinese history, computer vision)
Which stage is this topic for?
What research type do you lean toward?
options: not sure yet, help me decide

questions.question: How much time do you have for research and writing?
What level or type is the target journal or fund? (e.g. CSSCI, regular core journal, SCI Q3, university-level student innovation project)
What tone do you want for the topic and writing?
What topics or fields genuinely interest you and that you would want to spend long hours on? (They can look unrelated to your major, e.g. video games, cat ownership, band culture)
What resources do you already have? (e.g. datasets you can access, fieldwork or interview channels, lab equipment, methods you already know, your advisor's projects)
What hard constraints must be met? (e.g. the advisor has fixed the direction, questionnaire method is required, must use a specific company as a case)
Which directions do you explicitly want to avoid or rule out?

skip_logic.description: Skip questions that do not apply based on earlier answers, add level-specific questions, and bound the scope of the output.
rules: If the user picks "course paper", do not ask PhD-level theoretical contribution requirements and do not add a "theoretical innovation requirements" field to the output
If the user picks "journal submission" or "grant application", skip the length and timeline questions and instead ask about the target journal or fund level
If the user picks "master's thesis" or "PhD thesis" with a "light and humorous" tone, note in the risk warnings that the humor must stay within what the advisor and reviewers will accept
If the user already states an existing dataset or fieldwork channel in resources, do not ask again about data availability; reuse that resource when generating topics
If the user picks "not sure yet, help me decide" for research type, ask about method preferences based on discipline and resources in Step 3, then work back to feasible methods

tone_examples: Good: This topic focuses on the behavior of a specific user group, has a testable research hypothesis, and fills a clear gap in the existing literature.
Good: This study uses three middle schools in XX city as cases; the findings are limited in scope, and this limitation will be stated in the research design.
Bad: This topic is super fun, it will definitely go viral, you will pass for sure!
Bad: Everyone is talking about large models right now, so let us just write about how large models change the world.
conditional_notes: When the questionnaire tone is "a bit of humor allowed", metaphors may appear only in the title and introduction; the argument itself must stay rigorous.
When the tone is "light and humorous", humor may serve the way the question is framed but must not weaken the seriousness of the methods, evidence and conclusions.

constraint_list: There must be a specific, identifiable research object; broad unbounded fields are not accepted
The output unit must be a well-defined question (not a broad topic); the question must be answerable and falsifiable
The methods must be workable and match the research question
The study must be feasible within the user's level, length, timeline and resources
It must add academic value: at least one of a new object, a new angle, a new method or new evidence
It must give searchable entry points (keywords plus suggested databases or platforms); no fabricated literature or data
It must follow academic norms: citations, ethics review (when human subjects are involved) and informed consent
exclusion_rules: Pure literature reviews or rewrites with no new contribution
Areas with too many papers in the last three years, saturation above 80%, and no new angle or method
Topics beyond the current level's ability and resources (e.g. an undergraduate without technical skills or datasets attempting a large system)
Keyword-stuffed titles: hot terms spliced together with no real question
False-problem titles: the question does not hold or cannot be falsified
Directions the user explicitly lists in excludes
Research with ethics or compliance risks that cannot be mitigated by study design

output_format_adjustments.title_format: "{specific question}: a case study of {research object}"
